topic: The Magic of Convolution: Adding Random Variables
target_audience: University students in STEM (Statistics, Engineering, Data Science)

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Independent Duo
lecture_lines: Start with two independent random variables, X and Y.
We want to find the sum of their distributions.
Let's visualize this relationship on a 2D grid.
animations: Show two icons representing Alice (X) [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/alice.svg] and Bob (Y) in #ADD8E6 and #FFB6C1.
Fade in the equation 'Z = X + Y' in #FFFFFF at the top center.
Draw a 2D coordinate grid with X and Y axes; highlight cells in #FFFFE0.

sections.title: The Discrete Case: The 'Sum-to-K' Logic
lecture_lines: To find the probability that Z equals z.
If X equals k, Y must be z minus k.
This creates a diagonal line across our grid.
Sum all probabilities of pairs along this diagonal.
Moving the diagonal covers every possible sum.
animations: Highlight a specific cell (k, z-k) in the grid with #00FF00.
Display the equation 'x + y = z' near the grid in #FFFFFF.
Draw a diagonal line across all cells where x + y = z in #FFA500.

sections.title: Defining Convolution: Flip and Slide
lecture_lines: The discrete convolution formula defines this sum.
We sum P(X=k) times P(Y=z-k).
This is known as the "Flip and Slide" method.
Flip one distribution and slide it across another.
Overlapping values are multiplied and then summed together.
animations: Display the discrete convolution formula P(Z=z) = Σ P(X=k)P(Y=z-k) in #FFFFFF.
Show two bar charts; flip the second chart (Y) horizontally in #FFB6C1.
Slide the flipped chart Y across chart X, highlighting overlaps in #FFFF00.

sections.title: Transition to Continuous: The Convolution Integral
lecture_lines: For continuous variables, we use the convolution integral.
It calculates the probability density of the sum.
Visualize two smooth Bell curves passing through each other.
The area of their overlap determines the sum's PDF.
This integral formalizes the "Flip and Slide" intuition.
animations: Morph the summation symbol Σ into an integral sign ∫ in #FFFFFF.
Display two smooth Bell curves (Gaussians) in #ADD8E6 and #FFB6C1.
Slide one Bell curve over the other and shade the overlapping area in #00FFFF.

sections.title: Visual Summary: Why Convolution Matters
lecture_lines: Convolving distributions usually makes them smoother and wider.
Square distributions convolve into triangles, then bell curves.
This process reveals why the Normal distribution is common.
animations: Start with two uniform 'square' distributions in #FFFFFF.
Animate the convolution of squares into a triangle, then into a curve.
Repeatedly convolve to show the convergence to a golden Bell curve in #FFD700.
